# Source profile: AEMO half-hourly operational demand

*Generated by `scripts/profile.py` from `data/demand_halfhourly.csv.gz` (SHA-256 `694167b10ca3…`,
679,200 rows). Do not edit by hand.*

Times are NEM time (AEST, UTC+10, no daylight saving). A half-hour belongs to the day and time it
starts in. Calendar years 2019-2025 are complete; 2026 (Jan-Sep) is left out of
year-on-year tables.

## 1. Coverage and integrity

465 monthly files (5 regions x 93 months, Jan 2019 - Sep 2026),
every one matching its pinned SHA-256 in `data/raw_manifest.json`.
They hold 240,960 thirty-minute rows (to Sep 2021) and
2,629,440 five-minute rows (from Oct 2021), with
0 exact duplicate rows. Period types: `TRADE` (2,870,400).

Rolled up to half-hours, each region should have 135,840 rows. Result: **no missing half-hours**, and
every 5-minute half-hour has all 6 intervals.

| Region | Half-hours | Missing | Short (5-min era) | Min MW | Max MW |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 135,840 | 0 | 0 | 2,581.8 | 13,715.6 |
| QLD1 | 135,840 | 0 | 0 | 2,728.1 | 11,130.2 |
| VIC1 | 135,840 | 0 | 0 | 1,243.5 | 10,640.0 |
| SA1 | 135,840 | 0 | 0 | -283.7 | 3,308.5 |
| TAS1 | 135,840 | 0 | 0 | 508.2 | 1,758.3 |

The 5-minute and 30-minute eras are averaged the same way (time-weighted mean MW), so the
switch to five-minute settlement on 1 Oct 2021 doesn't change what a half-hour means.

The minimums move far more than the totals. Annual energy changed by
-5.9% to +1.8% between 2019 and
2025, but the lowest half-hour fell in every region, by as much as
**59% in VIC1** among regions still above zero. SA1's minimum first went **below zero in 2021** (in this data, which starts in 2019) and reached -284 MW in 2025: in those half-hours rooftop solar and other small generation inside the region more than covered its own use, so the surplus flowed back into the transmission network. In 2025
the year's lowest half-hour started in the middle of the day (10:00-16:00) in
**5 of 5 regions** (NSW1, QLD1, VIC1, SA1, TAS1).
Lowest half-hour, 2025 (start, NEM time): NSW1 16 Feb 12:00; QLD1 31 Aug 11:00; VIC1 27 Dec 12:30; SA1 25 Dec 13:30; TAS1 02 Nov 11:30.
Highest half-hour, 2025: NSW1 01 Jul 17:30; QLD1 22 Jan 17:30; VIC1 03 Feb 18:30; SA1 12 Feb 18:30; TAS1 01 Jul 08:00.

## 3. The midday trough: rooftop solar is reshaping the day

Operational demand is what the grid supplies, so every rooftop panel that generates at noon
removes demand the grid used to see. Two measures, weekdays and weekends combined unless noted:

Share of days whose lowest half-hour starts between 10:00 and 16:00 (NEM time):

| Region | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 4% | 7% | 27% | 37% | 57% | 58% | 66% |
| QLD1 | 21% | 36% | 53% | 56% | 72% | 65% | 76% |
| VIC1 | 11% | 24% | 37% | 40% | 56% | 66% | 70% |
| SA1 | 67% | 83% | 88% | 88% | 92% | 92% | 92% |
| TAS1 | 11% | 15% | 21% | 28% | 35% | 49% | 53% |

Weekday demand between 10:00 and 16:00 as a share of the weekday all-day average:

| Region | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 102% | 99% | 96% | 95% | 91% | 90% | 89% |
| QLD1 | 99% | 97% | 94% | 92% | 90% | 90% | 87% |
| VIC1 | 102% | 99% | 96% | 96% | 91% | 88% | 86% |
| SA1 | 87% | 79% | 74% | 75% | 68% | 65% | 62% |
| TAS1 | 98% | 98% | 97% | 97% | 96% | 95% | 94% |

In 2025, **SA1's demand bottomed out in the middle of the day on
92% of days** (vs 67% in 2019).
The share rose in 5 of 5 regions. Ranked by
2025: SA1 92%, QLD1 76%, VIC1 70%, NSW1 66%, TAS1 53%.

## 4. Seasons and weekends

Month of each year's highest half-hour:

| Region | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | Jan | Feb | Jun | Feb | Mar | Feb | Jul |
| QLD1 | Feb | Feb | Feb | Mar | Mar | Jan | Jan |
| VIC1 | Mar | Jan | Jan | Jan | Jan | Dec | Feb |
| SA1 | Dec | Jan | Feb | Dec | Feb | Mar | Feb |
| TAS1 | Jun | Aug | Aug | Jun | Jun | Jul | Jul |

Average daily peak by season (2019-2025, summer = Dec-Feb, winter = Jun-Aug) and the
weekend effect (2025: weekend average demand vs weekday):

| Region | Summer daily peak MW | Winter daily peak MW | Higher season | Weekend vs weekday |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 9,304 | 10,718 | winter | -7.4% |
| QLD1 | 8,252 | 7,513 | summer | -5.8% |
| VIC1 | 5,741 | 6,903 | winter | -9.7% |
| SA1 | 1,735 | 2,043 | winter | -7.7% |
| TAS1 | 1,170 | 1,468 | winter | -2.6% |

Average daily peaks are higher in winter in **4 of 5 regions**
(NSW1, VIC1, SA1, TAS1). Yet on the mainland the single highest half-hour of the year fell in
Dec-Mar in **26 of 28 region-years**: winter lifts the typical day, while
summer sets the record. A planner needs both numbers. Weekend demand runs
3%-10% below weekdays, so a forecast that
ignores the day of the week starts out wrong.

## 5. Context: negative prices

Share of half-hours with a negative average price, and (last column) the share of 2025's
negative-price half-hours that start between 10:00 and 16:00, a quarter of the day:

| Region | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | 2025: at 10:00-16:00 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NSW1 | 0.0% | 0.2% | 2.4% | 2.9% | 6.0% | 7.3% | 13.1% | 68% |
| QLD1 | 1.4% | 3.7% | 5.8% | 4.4% | 13.2% | 13.9% | 19.5% | 67% |
| VIC1 | 0.7% | 4.4% | 15.4% | 14.7% | 23.2% | 22.7% | 24.1% | 52% |
| SA1 | 4.5% | 9.8% | 19.4% | 19.0% | 26.2% | 26.0% | 30.4% | 51% |
| TAS1 | 1.2% | 2.8% | 10.5% | 1.9% | 7.3% | 7.3% | 3.8% | 52% |

In 2025, SA1 had a negative price in 30% of half-hours, and
51%-68% of each region's negative-price
half-hours fell in that midday window. Low midday demand and cheap midday power go together, which
is why the shape of the day, and not only the peak, matters to anyone buying or scheduling around
demand.

## What this means for forecasting

- **The data is clean enough to forecast from as is**: no gaps to fill, no conflicting duplicates,
  and one consistent half-hourly grain across the 2021 switch to five-minute settlement.
- **Three cycles to capture**: time of day, day of week (weekends run
  3%-10% lower) and season
  (winter-led in 4 of 5 regions). A baseline that ignores one of
  them is a straw man.
- **History ages fast**: the midday shape in 2025 isn't the shape of 2019, so methods
  that weight recent weeks (seasonal naive, exponential smoothing) should beat long-run averages.
  Part 2 tests that with a rolling-origin backtest rather than assuming it.
- **The minimum is now a planning problem too**: in 5 of 5 regions
  the lowest half-hour of 2025 came at midday, so forecast accuracy should be judged at the
  trough as well as the peak.
